topic: Snapshots and Copy-on-Write: The Economics of Agent Sandboxes
keyword: snapshots copy on write agent sandbox economics

key_points: The exact topic article: how Cortex crammed thousands of isolated agents onto a single machine using Firecracker microVMs.
A minimal microVM is NOT a minimal workload: a 4 GiB guest can pull several GiB of pages into host RAM once a compiler, language server, browser, and build daemon start.
Copying a 40 GiB ext4 image per agent is absurd when most agents change only a few files.
Fleet cost model: cost = t(alpha*vCPU + beta*RAM + gamma*Disk) * n; 9-24 parallel agents saturate a host before autoscaling.
Ephemeral one-shot sandboxes (like Stripe's CI-style contract) don't fit harness-agnostic long-lived sessions where you resume months later.

Snapshot approach: Firecracker serializes vCPU/KVM/device state into state.bin, guest memory into mem.bin, disk as a file. But combined snapshots are MASSIVE (16 GiB RAM + 128 GiB disk = ~144 GiB worst case).
Solution: split disk into fixed 16 MiB chunks, SHA-256 hash each, content-addressable storage; identical chunks stored once, zeroed chunks skipped; manifest maps offsets to hashes.
NBD (Network Block Device) server bridges content-addressed storage to Firecracker; reads fetch chunks on demand, NVMe as LRU hot-chunk cache.
Copy-on-write: first write to an immutable base chunk creates a private dirty copy; one write = one new chunk; a session dirtying 20 chunks adds at most 320 MiB even on a 128 GiB disk.

Memory: content-address in 512 KiB chunks; base shm file mapped with MAP_PRIVATE so clean pages share page-cache backing, writes get private pages via kernel CoW; userfaultfd fills sparse base shm on demand (UFFDIO_CONTINUE preserves sharing).
Result: cost shifts from cost ∝ requested(vCPU+RAM+disk) to cost ∝ alpha*vCPU + beta*(base shm + dirty RAM) + gamma*(base disk + dirty disk).
Idle sandboxes can be captured and evicted, autoscaler removes empty hosts; size for active work, not every retained session.
Why agents need sandboxes: an AI coding agent runs commands you didn't write; exploits range from rm -rf to hijacking credentials.
Allow/deny command lists are non-starters at scale due to combinatorial explosion; Claude Code 'auto mode' secondary classifier is still a black box.
Solution at scale: give each agent its own throwaway Linux box with strict egress policies; treat each agent as potentially adversarial and eliminate blast radius.
Firecracker is a lightweight VMM using Linux KVM; minimal device model (no full PC emulation) gives fast boot and low overhead.
A freshly-booted microVM is a sealed box: no screen, keyboard, or network until you wire it up.
Kernel-level sandboxing: file hiding through the Linux open syscall; assume whatever the process can 'see' it can send to the user.
Application-level safeguards are insufficient; the kernel should say 'no' (do_open -EACCES, link_path_walk, path_init failure modes).
Run agents inside containers so the kernel enforces the boundary, not app code.
Hosting an agent on a cloud machine opens a dangerous attack surface vs. running locally.

2026 sandbox ecosystem mapped structurally into layers: primitives (Firecracker/gVisor/LiteBox), embeddable runtimes (E2B, microsandbox), managed platforms (Daytona, Modal, Northflank), hybrid (Google Agent Sandbox).
Standard multi-tenant containers can't safely contain AI agents executing arbitrary code; shared kernel surface is a liability.
AWS, Azure, GCP have all migrated control planes away from runc toward hardware-enforced isolation.
Five isolation levels: (1) containers, (2) user-space kernels gVisor, (3) micro-VMs Firecracker/Kata/libkrun, (4) library OS LiteBox, (5) confidential computing AMD SEV-SNP/Intel TDX.
Firecracker boots in ~125ms with ~5MB memory overhead; powers AWS Lambda, E2B, Vercel Sandbox.
Security is a spectrum: internal code = containers fine; LLM-generated code = gVisor or microVMs; user-uploaded binaries = assume hostile, hardware virtualization.
Hyperscaler signal: AWS built Firecracker for Lambda, Google built gVisor for Search/Gmail, Azure uses Hyper-V for ephemeral agent sandboxes.
Sandboxing agents is at least two problems: local (developer machine) vs remote (multi-tenant) sandboxes have different threat models and controls.
Local sandbox: confused deputy risk (prompt injection, poisoned MCP context, hallucination); controls = workspace boundaries, secret isolation, network egress policy, visibility/reversibility.
Remote sandbox: adversarial workloads; controls = isolation boundaries with defense in depth, no secrets in the sandbox, egress as chokepoint, resource/cost governance, ephemerality.
A sandbox that's too annoying gets disabled, which is worse than none (false sense of security).
Remote sandboxing is about ensuring bad behavior cannot become a systemic incident.

angles: The core economic insight: sandbox cost should scale with what an agent actually uses (base image + divergences), not with what it requests — 'pay for divergence, not for the whole VM'.
Content-addressable storage + copy-on-write turns a 128 GiB disk into a manifest of shared immutable chunks; identical bytes are stored once across all sandboxes.
Memory is the harder problem than disk: no NBD boundary to resolve reads, so MAP_PRIVATE + userfaultfd (UFFDIO_CONTINUE) is needed to keep clean pages shared while writes stay private.
Session density vs resource density: snapshot-and-evict idle sandboxes so you size for active work, not every retained session — agents spend most time waiting on humans/network.
The 'ephemeral one-shot' (CI-style) contract works for Stripe but fails harness-agnostic long-lived sessions where you resume months later — full state recovery (memory, disk, processes) is the goal.
Isolation is a spectrum (containers → gVisor → microVMs → library OS → confidential computing); the right choice depends on trust, latency, data, and compliance.
Local vs remote sandboxing are two different problems with different threat models (confused deputy vs adversarial tenant) and different controls.
Hyperscaler signal is unambiguous: every major cloud built its strongest isolation primitive and pointed it at AI — none reached for containers.
